raw_response.country: 62 low- and middle-income countries (most frequently India, Kenya and Bangladesh)

criterion_notes.c1: Topically covers water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH) interventions in household (56.8%) and community (25.3%) settings, coding whether mapped studies addressed equitable access and use of safe water supply (41.3%), safe sanitation (31.1%), service quality (29.4%) and affordability (19.9%).
criterion_notes.c2: Fails both the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading and the plain wording of Criterion 2. Under the narrow 2026-10-13 reading, the review does not examine a rule-type legal, administrative or regulatory mechanism directly governing service access (such as eligibility screening, administrative burden, documentation or tenure requirements, tariff or cost-recovery rules, discretion/accommodation, enforcement, or utility regulatory structure); instead, its exposure scope is generic WASH project delivery and behavioural promotion (behaviour change interventions 50.5%, WASH infrastructure provision 40%, training and capacity building 24.8%). Under the plain wording of Criterion 2, it also does not examine a legal, administrative, institutional, regulatory or governance factor governing access: WASH interventions are treated as the independent variable to map gender equality and social inclusion (GESI) outcomes, and items such as participation in decision-making or financial support (tariffs, loans and subsidies, tagged in 13.5% of the 104 GESI-mainstreamed studies) appear only as unanalysed metadata counts without any governance or institutional analysis.
criterion_notes.c3: Although the paper uses systematic search and screening methods across 463 primary studies, it is a systematic evidence map rather than a primary empirical study or a systematic empirical synthesis of study findings: the authors explicitly state that no critical appraisal and no data extraction of study results were conducted, and only bibliographic/intervention metadata frequencies were coded and narratively described.
criterion_notes.c4: Does not report empirical outcomes or synthesised findings on water or sanitation access, connection, availability, reliability, quantity, affordability or exclusion; it reports only bibliometric counts of how many primary studies measured 25 GESI outcome themes, and explicitly notes it was not set up to evaluate the impacts of WASH interventions on outcomes.
criterion_notes.c5: The unit of analysis is the published or grey-literature study record (463 studies across 499 publications) coded at the metadata level; because primary findings and exposure-outcome relationships were not extracted, household- or community-level legal/administrative exposures and service-access outcomes are not identifiable.
criterion_notes.c6: Published in English in BMJ Global Health.

evidence_quotes.quote: WASH interventions implemented in households, schools, health facilities, community spaces and workplace settings were considered eligible for this review.
What evidence exists on the GESI outcomes of WASH interventions in low-income and mid-income contexts?
A little over half of all studies involved behaviour change interventions (50.5%), followed by interventions that provided WASH infrastructure (40%) and training and capacity building (24.8%)
However, no critical appraisal and data extraction was conducted in this review. We undertook a systematic mapping of the primary research studies instead.

evidence_quotes.page: PDF Page 4 (Methods - Metadata extraction and synthesis)
evidence_quotes.quote: The metadata from each record was then extracted by a single reviewer and the metadata was then narratively synthesised to assess frequencies and trends in the evidence base.
This systematic map was also not set to evaluate the impacts of WASH interventions on GESI outcomes, but the evidence collated in this work provides a basis for such investigations.

raw_response.exposure: WASH interventions broadly (behaviour change programmes 50.5%, WASH infrastructure provision 40%, training and capacity building 24.8%), including GESI mainstreaming components in 22% (104/463) of mapped studies
raw_response.outcome: Bibliometric frequencies of 25 coded GESI outcome themes reported across mapped studies (12 inclusive themes such as equitable WASH access/use and affordability, and 13 transformative themes such as time use, participation and empowerment); no primary empirical outcome results or intervention effects extracted
raw_response.population_and_sample: 463 primary WASH intervention studies (across 499 publications) published 2010–2020 in low- and middle-income countries, covering interventions in households (56.8%), communities (25.3%), schools (19.4%) and individuals (10.8%)
raw_response.rationale: Excluded primarily for wrong exposure (E03), and secondarily because it is a bibliometric systematic evidence map that extracts no empirical findings on service access outcomes. First, on Criterion 2, the review maps generic WASH project interventions (behaviour change/messaging 50.5%, infrastructure provision 40%, training and capacity building 24.8%) as the exposure to catalogue gender equality and social inclusion (GESI) outcomes, rather than examining a legal, administrative, regulatory or rule-type mechanism governing water or sanitation service access (failing both the 2026-10-13 rule-type reading and the plain wording of Criterion 2). Second, on Criteria 3–5, the authors explicitly conducted no critical appraisal or data extraction of primary study findings, reporting only metadata counts of study characteristics and outcome themes rather than synthesising empirical evidence on water or sanitation access outcomes.
raw_response.study_design: Systematic mapping review (evidence map with bibliographic metadata coding and narrative synthesis of study frequencies; no critical appraisal or outcome data extraction)
